title: Two bike-share firms in a payoff matrix, then a monopoly with a lump-sum fee
scenario: Pedalwise and Sunpath (invented) are the only bike-share firms in a city. Each decides, at the same time and without talking to the other, whether to expand into a new district (Expand) or stay in its current districts (Stay). The matrix shows each firm's monthly profit in thousands of dollars; in each cell Pedalwise's payoff is listed first. Both firms know the matrix.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify each firm's dominant strategy, if it has one, and every Nash equilibrium.

rubric.point: Pedalwise's dominant strategy is Expand, and Sunpath has no dominant strategy.
The only Nash equilibrium is (Pedalwise Expand, Sunpath Stay).

parts.sample: Pedalwise's dominant strategy is Expand. Sunpath has no dominant strategy. The only Nash equilibrium is Pedalwise Expand, Sunpath Stay, with payoffs of \$70 thousand and \$25 thousand.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain, using the numbers in the matrix, why Sunpath does not have a dominant strategy.

rubric.point: Gives both comparisons for Sunpath: if Pedalwise expands, Stay is better (25 > 10); if Pedalwise stays, Expand is better (50 > 48). So its best choice depends on Pedalwise's.

parts.sample: If Pedalwise chooses Expand, Sunpath earns 10 from Expand and 25 from Stay, so Stay is better. If Pedalwise chooses Stay, Sunpath earns 50 from Expand and 48 from Stay, so Expand is better. Sunpath's best choice changes with Pedalwise's choice, so it has no dominant strategy.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The city now pays Sunpath a subsidy of \$20 thousand a month whenever it chooses Expand. Identify each firm's dominant strategy, if any, after the subsidy.

rubric.point: Sunpath's dominant strategy is now Expand (30 > 25 and 70 > 48), and Pedalwise's is still Expand.

parts.sample: Sunpath's Expand payoffs rise to 30 and 70. Expand now beats Stay whatever Pedalwise does (30 > 25 and 70 > 48), so Expand is Sunpath's dominant strategy. Pedalwise's payoffs did not change, so Expand is still its dominant strategy.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Later, Pedalwise buys Sunpath and becomes the only bike-share firm in the city, earning a positive economic profit. Draw a correctly labeled graph for Pedalwise showing demand, marginal revenue, marginal cost and average total cost, and show its profit-maximizing price and quantity, labeled PM and QM.

rubric.point: A correctly labeled monopoly graph: axes, downward-sloping D, MR below D, MC crossing ATC at the minimum of ATC.
QM where MR = MC and PM on the demand curve above QM, with PM above ATC at QM.
accept: dotted lines from demand to both axes

parts.sample: Price and cost on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal. D slopes down, MR lies below it, MC crosses ATC at its minimum. QM is where MR = MC; PM is read straight up on the demand curve, above ATC at QM.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The city charges Pedalwise a lump-sum license fee each year, the same whatever number of rides it provides. Show the effect of the fee on your graph by shifting the curve or curves that change.

key.because: a lump-sum license fee (a fixed cost)

rubric.point: Shifts ATC up and leaves MC (and D and MR) unchanged.
accept: ATC2 drawn above ATC1, MC unchanged

parts.sample: ATC shifts up to ATC2. MC, demand and MR do not move.

parts.label: F(i)
parts.prompt: Identify the effect of the lump-sum fee on Pedalwise's profit-maximizing quantity and price.

rubric.point: Both the quantity and the price stay the same.
accept: no change in QM or PM

parts.sample: Pedalwise's profit-maximizing quantity and price do not change.

parts.label: F(ii)

rubric.point: Explains that the fee is a fixed cost, so it does not change marginal cost; MR and MC still cross at the same quantity, and the price on demand at that quantity is the same (only profit falls).
accept: MC does not change, so MR = MC at the same quantity

parts.sample: The lump-sum fee does not depend on how many rides Pedalwise provides, so it is a fixed cost: it raises ATC but leaves MC unchanged. MR still equals MC at the same quantity, and the price read from demand at that quantity is the same. Only Pedalwise's profit falls, by the amount of the fee.

parts.label: G
parts.prompt: Shade the deadweight loss that results from Pedalwise's monopoly.

rubric.point: Shades the area between demand and MC, from QM to the quantity where demand meets MC.
accept: the triangle between D and MC to the right of QM

parts.sample: The deadweight loss is the triangle between the demand curve and MC, from QM to the quantity where demand meets MC.
